text: That's why I'd tell everyone not to dance on MDMA at all, however good the music is, since dancing makes the heat and the sweat that drain their salt. And really, what's the point of MDMA if someone wants to dance? For that they can take some San Pedro cactus or mescaline, which is way way safer, and still very therapeutic. Real MDMA, the kind that's therapeutic and helps people access very early childhood trauma, possibly better than San Pedro can in some cases, isn't the kind people want to dance on, which is why you don't see people in the MAPS trials of MDMA therapy saying "I NEED TO DANCE!" No, they're sitting there doing the therapy, and even if the science isn't clear on this yet, I and everyone I know are totally clear about what the real thing feels like. It's not like "I don't feel like dancing", it's like "I can barely move", couch lock. And in the same exact setting, the pills have gone both ways on me: some had me wanting to dance, and some left me in that couch lock. So if a pill makes someone feel like dancing, I'm highly suspicious that it contains amphetamines, or that it isn't real MDMA at all, maybe 6-APB, a similar drug. That might also be why women get low sodium far more often than men outside the lab, where what people take as "MDMA" is ecstasy, while a [lab study](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4923534/) that gave people pure MDMA and water found no difference between them. Then again, the lab dosed everyone by their weight, and at a festival a small woman takes the same pill as a big guy, so she's getting a lot more for her size.
reader: someone about to go to a festival with friends who plan to take MDMA and dance all night, reading this the day before

question_text.Q1: Why am I reading this sentence, and do I know it before I have to work through it? (the point first, in each sentence and each paragraph; a study after the question it answers; a term explained where it is first used, never in a sentence after it)
question_text.Q2: What is each instruction for, said in the reader's terms, and is it something the helper does ("have someone go with them"), not a rule stated as a fact ("someone goes with them")?
question_text.Q3: Which thing exactly? (pools of water, not water; any substance, not anything)
question_text.Q4: What does each word act on, or mean here? (adjunct remedy; known-genuine) Is every term a high-school graduate wouldn't know (enterocytes, BPC-157) explained once, where it is first used, and common ones (a vitamin) left alone? Is each mechanism explained by what it does in the reader's experience (dopamine "for motivation (by showing us what is important to pay attention to)"; DeltaFosB "preventing that learning from really clicking"), not by where it sits or what it looks like ("a chemical blanket", "the slower one underneath")? question_text.Q6: Is this the order the reader is thinking in, and does each idea sit next to what it continues?
